summary: For ages 12–13, teach hurricanes, tornadoes and monsoons as three distinct physical engines rather than a list of scary events: a hurricane runs on latent heat released when water evaporated from a warm (>~26–27 °C) ocean condenses aloft, deepening a low-pressure spiral spun by the Coriolis effect (so they almost never form within about 5° of the equator); a tornado is a much smaller, faster-forming funnel that can form when horizontal spin created by wind shear is tilted upright by a supercell thunderstorm's updraft and stretched; a monsoon is a continent-scale seasonal reversal of winds driven by land and sea heating and cooling at different rates (both a wet and a dry phase). Finish with attribution science honestly: a warmer ocean and atmosphere load the dice toward heavier rain, stronger storms and higher surge, shifting probability and intensity for a class of events without any single storm being simply 'caused' by climate change. Prioritise manipulation and prediction so children feel each engine, then consolidate the scale/mechanism contrasts and the attribution logic.
misconceptions: Lumping all violent weather together — thinking hurricanes and tornadoes are the same thing or that a hurricane is just a big tornado; they differ hugely in scale, formation and energy source.

Believing a single hurricane or heatwave was 'caused by climate change' (or, conversely, that because such storms always existed, warming has no effect); the accurate idea is probability-shifting/dice-loading.
Thinking a hurricane's power comes mainly from wind pushing water, missing that its energy source is latent heat released when evaporated ocean water condenses.
Assuming hurricanes can form anywhere warm, including on the equator; they need Coriolis to spin, which is zero at the equator.
Thinking monsoon = simply 'the rainy season/lots of rain' rather than a seasonal REVERSAL of winds driven by land–sea heating contrast (with both a wet and a dry phase).

activities.title: Spin up a storm: the hurricane engine
steps: Take the controls of a storm-building model and accept the challenge: 'make a hurricane spin up.'
Start over a cool ocean — observe that only a few clouds appear and no storm organises.

Raise sea-surface temperature past ~27 °C, add moisture, and keep wind shear low; watch moist air rise, a 'latent heat released' gauge surge as vapour condenses high up, the core pressure drop, and a spiral with a clean eye organise.
Try to build the same storm right on the equator and observe it refuse to spin; then move a working storm over land or cool water and watch it starve and weaken.
State in your own words which ingredient each failure removed (warm water, moisture, low shear, distance from the equator).
activities.insight: A hurricane's power is not the wind pushing water — it is the latent heat released when evaporated seawater condenses aloft, which warms the core, deepens the low-pressure spiral and intensifies the storm; and it needs the Coriolis effect to rotate, so it almost never forms within about 5° of the equator, and it weakens and eventually decays once cut off from warm ocean.

activities.title: Flip the monsoon: land and sea heating
steps: Use a land–sea panel with a season toggle; begin from the day/land-sea breeze idea the learner may already know (land heats faster by day, drawing a sea breeze).
Toggle to summer: observe land heating faster, forming lower pressure, and moist onshore winds bringing the wet season.
Toggle to winter: observe the pressure gradient and winds reverse to give the dry season.
Describe explicitly what flips between summer and winter and why — naming the land–sea temperature/pressure difference as the cause.
State a one-sentence definition that a monsoon is a seasonal reversal with both wet and dry phases, not just 'the rainy season.'
activities.insight: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by land and sea heating and cooling at different rates, producing distinct wet and dry seasons in many regions such as much of South Asia — a similar differential-heating principle to a daily land–sea breeze, but at continental scale over a season, where Earth's rotation and the seasonal shift of tropical rain belts also matter.

activities.title: Build a tornado inside a supercell
steps: Work in a supercell mode: adjust vertical wind shear and instability.

Increase shear to create horizontally spinning air, then watch the supercell's updraft tilt it upright into a rotating mesocyclone that can be stretched into a narrow, fast funnel — noting that most supercells do not produce a tornado.

Compare directly with the hurricane mode: note the tornado is typically tens to hundreds of metres wide and forms in minutes, usually over land inside a thunderstorm, whereas the hurricane is hundreds of kilometres across and forms over days over warm ocean.
State the different energy source and scale for each in one sentence.
activities.insight: A tornado is a much smaller-scale funnel (typically tens to hundreds of metres, forming in minutes) that can form when horizontal spin created by wind shear is tilted upright by a supercell thunderstorm's updraft and stretched, usually over land — a distinct mechanism, scale and speed from a warm-ocean, latent-heat-driven hurricane.

activities.title: Loaded dice: attribution science
steps: Turn on an attribution overlay that warms the baseline ocean by about a degree and shows the intensity distribution of storms sliding toward stronger events.
Observe that not every storm becomes worse — the odds shift, like loaded dice.

Read a headline such as 'Climate change caused this storm' and rewrite it the way an attribution scientist would (e.g. 'this class of event became X times more likely / Y% heavier rainfall because of warming').
Answer the probe questions: why do hurricanes weaken rapidly after landfall; how is 'made 3 times more likely' different from 'caused'; and what flips in a monsoon and why.

Optionally interview an in-role attribution scientist or hurricane forecaster about how storms get their energy, why the equator is off-limits, and how scientists discuss a storm's link to a warming climate without overclaiming.
activities.insight: Attribution science uses climate models to estimate whether and how much warming changed the likelihood or intensity of a class of extreme events (often making heat and heavy-rain extremes more likely or intense) — a probability/intensity shift ('loaded dice'), not a claim that a single storm was simply caused by climate change.

activities.title: Sort and sequence: consolidate the three engines
steps: Sort features into hurricane / tornado / monsoon categories (e.g. warm-ocean latent-heat engine, supercell shear funnel, seasonal land–sea reversal, continent-scale, tens of metres, forms in minutes, forms over days).
Answer focused questions: what is a hurricane's energy source; why do almost none form near the equator; and why is attribution 'dice-loading' rather than single-event cause.
Order the hurricane formation chain: warm sea → evaporation → condensation → latent heat released → falling core pressure → spin.
Set a slider to the minimum sea-surface temperature needed for hurricane formation (~26–27 °C).
activities.insight: The learner can independently discriminate the three systems by mechanism and scale, recall the hurricane ingredient set and the Coriolis/equator point, and state the attribution logic.

checkQuestion: After a record-breaking hurricane, a headline reads 'Climate change caused this storm.' An attribution scientist would phrase it more carefully. What does attribution science actually let us say about the link between climate change and a single extreme event — and what is the ocean's warmth doing to power a hurricane in the first place?
checkAnswer: Attribution science doesn't say a single event was simply 'caused' by climate change; using climate models it estimates how much more likely or more intense that class of event became because of warming (e.g. '3× more likely,' '10% heavier rain'). The hurricane is powered by warm ocean water evaporating; when that vapour condenses it releases latent heat, warming the core, deepening the low-pressure spiral and intensifying the storm.
